2024 · arXiv · Benchmarks & Evals

AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments

Instead of another static medical multiple-choice set, four LLM agents — doctor, patient, measurement, moderator — run a full simulated clinical encounter. The result: a model's standard MedQA score is a poor guide to how it performs once diagnosis requires asking the right questions in the right order.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By late 2023, LLM accuracy on the USMLE-style MedQA benchmark had climbed from 38.1% (Sept. 2021) to 90.2% (Nov. 2023) — above the reported human expert score of 87% and well clear of the 60% human passing bar. Read at face value, that trajectory says frontier LLMs have essentially solved medical diagnosis. AgentClinic's authors argue it says something much narrower: that LLMs are good at picking the right answer out of four or five choices when every symptom, lab value, and history detail needed to solve the case has already been assembled and handed to them in the prompt. Real clinical work is the opposite — a doctor starts with almost nothing (a chief complaint), has to decide which questions to ask and which tests to order under a finite budget of patient interactions, and only then reaches a diagnosis. None of that sequential, information-gathering structure is exercised by a static multiple-choice question.

Prior attempts to close this gap fall short in different ways: AMIE (Tu et al., 2024) simulates history-taking dialogue but is closed-source, doesn't let the model order tests or images, and isn't configurable for multimodal cases; CRAFT-MD (Johri et al., 2023) and SAPS (Liao et al., 2024) are similarly dialogue-based but don't cover bias, tool use, multiple languages, or specialties; and MedAgents (Tang et al., 2023) improves static QA accuracy through agent collaboration but never actually simulates a patient. AgentClinic's contribution is to put all of these pieces — patient interaction, tool use, medical imaging, cognitive/implicit bias injection, multilingual and multi-specialty coverage — into one open-source, dialogue-driven environment, and then show empirically that a model's static MedQA score barely predicts how it does once the format changes.

// how it works

The method

AgentClinic runs four LLM agents per case. The doctor agent is the model under evaluation: it starts with only a brief objective (e.g. "evaluate the patient presenting with chest pain") and must gather information through dialogue. The patient agent knows its own symptoms and history but not its diagnosis, and responds the way a real patient would. The measurement agent answers requests for exams and tests (temperature, EKG, an MRI reading) using the case's ground-truth findings. The moderator agent — an LLM given the correct diagnosis — parses whatever unstructured text the doctor eventually produces ("I believe a diagnosis of Type 2 Diabetes with possible insulin resistance is appropriate") and scores it right or wrong. The doctor is capped at N=20 patient/measurement interactions before it must commit to a diagnosis; each test request also counts against that budget, mirroring the finite-question constraint real physicians face.

Cases are drawn from five sources, populated into a structured JSON template (patient history, exam findings, ground-truth diagnosis) by GPT-4 and then manually validated: AgentClinic-MedQA (215 USMLE-derived cases), AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV (200 cases built from de-identified EHR data), AgentClinic-NEJM (120 multimodal cases sampled from 932 New England Journal of Medicine case challenges, each with real diagnostic images), AgentClinic-Spec (260 specialist cases across 9 specialties, from MedMCQA), and AgentClinic-Lang (749 AgentClinic-MedQA cases machine-translated into 6 additional languages and corrected by native speakers, covering Chinese, Hindi, Korean, Spanish, French, and Persian alongside English).

On top of the base setup, AgentClinic layers two evaluation axes that a static benchmark can't express. First, bias injection: the doctor or patient agent's system prompt can be seeded with any of a set of cognitive biases (recency, frequency, false-consensus, self-diagnosis, status-quo, confirmation) or implicit biases (race, gender, sexual orientation, religion, socioeconomic status, culture, education), so the effect of bias on both diagnostic accuracy and the patient's subjective experience can be measured directly in the dialogue rather than as a static prompt prefix. Second, an agent toolbox — Zero-Shot CoT, One-Shot CoT, Reflection CoT, Adaptive RAG over a medical textbook, Adaptive RAG over the web, and a persistent Notebook the doctor can write to and read from across cases — lets the benchmark measure whether standard agent scaffolding actually helps a given model in this setting.

// what they found

The results

Across 11 doctor models on AgentClinic-MedQA (each paired with a GPT-4 patient and measurement agent), Claude 3.5 Sonnet leads at 62.1% ± 3.3, followed by OpenBioLLM-70B at 58.3% ± 4.2 and three human physicians at 54% ± 28.5 (a small n=3 sample given the same 20-interaction budget). GPT-4 trails the humans at 51.6% ± 3.3, and accuracy falls off sharply from there: Mixtral-8x7B 37.1% ± 3.1, GPT-3.5 36.6%, GPT-4o 34.2% ± 3.4, MedLlama3-8B 31.4% ± 2.9, Meditron-70B 29.1% ± 2.4, PMC-Llama-7B 23.6% ± 2.1, Llama-3-70B 19.0% ± 2.5, down to Llama-2-70B-chat at just 4.5% ± 1.3. On AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV the ranking shuffles — OpenBioLLM-70B (38.1% ± 3.2) and PMC-Llama-7B (34.3% ± 3.0) hold up much better relative to GPT-4 (34.0% ± 3.1) than they do on MedQA, while Llama-3-70B falls to 8.5% ± 1.9.

The headline methodological finding is that MedQA accuracy is only weakly predictive of AgentClinic-MedQA accuracy: several models that score well on the original multiple-choice MedQA questions post far lower accuracy once the same cases are converted into sequential dialogue, with the paper reporting that diagnostic accuracy "can drop to below a tenth of the original accuracy" for the worst-affected models. Reducing the interaction budget compounds this — cutting N from 20 to 10 drops accuracy from roughly 52% to 25%, while the choice of patient-agent model also matters (a GPT-4 patient yields 52% doctor accuracy vs. 46% for a Mixtral patient), showing that a doctor model's measured accuracy is entangled with which model is playing the other three roles.

Breaking down performance by language, specialty, and tool use (AgentClinic-Lang, AgentClinic-Spec, and the tool study) tells a consistent story: Claude 3.5 Sonnet dominates almost every axis, averaging 66.7% across 9 specialties (peaking at 78.3% on Internal Medicine) and 48.4% across 7 languages — more than double the next-best model, GPT-4, at 20.9%. Other models degrade sharply outside English: GPT-4's accuracy on AgentClinic-Lang ranges from 40.18% (English) down to 11.21% (Chinese), and GPT-4o from 35.5% (English) to 3.73% (Korean). Tool benefit is likewise model-specific rather than universal: Claude 3.5 peaks at 56.1% with the Notebook tool, GPT-4 actually surpasses Claude 3.5 on Reflection CoT (42.2% vs. 40.2%), and Llama-3-70B gains the most from any single tool — Notebook takes it from a 21.4% baseline to 41.1%, a 92% relative improvement — while GPT-3.5 loses accuracy with every tool tested, its worst case (Adaptive RAG over a textbook) costing 9.2 points off its ~36% baseline.

On the multimodal AgentClinic-NEJM set (120 cases requiring both dialogue and reading a diagnostic image), Claude 3.5 Sonnet again leads at 37.2% ± 2.2 when the image is given upfront, ahead of GPT-4 (27.7% ± 2.0), GPT-4o (21.4% ± 1.7), and GPT-4o-mini (8.0% ± 1.2); accuracy for all four models drops slightly (to 35.4%, 25.4%, 19.1%, and 6.1% respectively) when the image must instead be requested from the measurement agent rather than being handed over at the start. Three clinician raters scoring 20 AgentClinic-MedQA dialogues gave average realism/quality scores of 6.2 (doctor), 6.7 (patient), 6.3 (measurement), and 5.8 (empathy) on a 1–10 scale — moderate marks, with reviewers specifically flagging poor opening statements and a lack of an empathetic opening question from the doctor agent.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

AgentClinic's central argument — that dialogue-based evaluation surfaces failure modes static MCQA hides — is well demonstrated by its own MedQA-vs-AgentClinic-MedQA comparison. But several aspects of how the benchmark itself is scored and validated deserve scrutiny before treating its leaderboard as ground truth about clinical capability.

The bias study is the sharpest illustration. It's run on only two of the eleven doctor models (GPT-4 and Mixtral-8x7B), so the striking finding — GPT-4's diagnostic accuracy barely moves under bias (normalized accuracy 92–98.6% across cognitive and implicit categories) while Mixtral-8x7B degrades much more unevenly (cognitive-bias normalized accuracy averaging 86.4% but ranging from 78.4% for the doctor agent to 94.5% for the patient agent, plus an 88.3% implicit-bias average) — tells us nothing directly about whether Claude 3.5 Sonnet, the model that actually tops every other leaderboard in the paper, is robust or fragile to the same biases. The paper's own explanation for GPT-4's apparent robustness undercuts it further: the authors report GPT-4 "verbosely rejected" a bias-instruction 25 times out of 215 gender-bias dialogues, and note this "does not mean that GPT-4 is free of said biases" — the accuracy metric may just be measuring refusal-to-role-play rather than genuine debiasing. Meanwhile the more clinically interesting signal — that implicit bias barely dents diagnostic accuracy but substantially lowers patient-reported confidence, compliance, and willingness to return — is real and important, but it's also self-reported by an LLM patient agent, not a human, so it measures how an LLM predicts a biased patient would feel rather than how one actually would.

baselines

11 doctor models span three tiers (frontier general-purpose, medical-finetuned 7–70B, and a 3-physician human baseline) which is a reasonable spread, but the human baseline (n=3, ±28.5 CI) is too small to support the headline "human physicians beat GPT-4" framing implied by the leaderboard position.

contamination

The paper explicitly flags that GPT-4/GPT-4o/GPT-3.5/Claude-3.5 may have trained on MedQA, and only two models (Mixtral-8x7B, Llama-2-70B-chat) are confirmed not to have; its sole counter-evidence is that MedQA accuracy doesn't predict AgentClinic-MedQA accuracy, which shows the two evaluations diverge but doesn't rule out leakage inflating either score individually.

what's missed

The moderator (LLM judge with ground truth) and the patient/measurement agents in almost every run are themselves GPT-4 — so a doctor model's score is partly a function of how well GPT-4-as-patient/grader interacts with it, a same-model-family confound the paper cites (Panickssery et al., 2024, on LLMs favoring their own outputs) but doesn't control for.

would raise confidence

Running the bias grid across all 11 models (especially Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o), reporting inter-rater agreement for the 3-clinician realism scores, and a direct contamination probe (e.g., canary strings or membership-inference on MedQA) rather than the indirect "weak correlation" argument.

// bottom line

The core methodological claim — that sequential dialogue diagnosis is a materially harder and differently-ranked task than static MedQA — is convincingly shown and is the paper's real contribution. The bias, tool, and multilingual sub-studies are valuable exploratory signal, but each is run on a small slice of the full model roster (2 models for bias; a handful for tools and language), self-graded or self-simulated in ways that intertwine the metric with the model playing the grader/patient, and validated by a 3-person human panel — so they should be read as suggestive findings to build on, not settled comparisons across the field's frontier models.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. AgentClinic replaces static medical MCQA with a four-agent (doctor/patient/measurement/moderator) simulated clinical encounter, and shows a model's MedQA score is only weakly predictive of its AgentClinic-MedQA score — some models drop to below a tenth of their static accuracy once diagnosis requires sequential information-gathering.
  2. Claude 3.5 Sonnet leads nearly every axis tested (models, specialties, languages, most tools), while medical-finetuned small models (MedLlama3-8B, PMC-Llama-7B) badly underperform general frontier models in dialogue despite reasonable static-QA performance — except OpenBioLLM-70B, which is competitive with GPT-4.
  3. Simulated bias barely dents diagnostic accuracy for GPT-4 but substantially lowers the patient agent's self-reported trust, compliance, and willingness to return — accuracy alone hides the harm, though the bias grid itself is only tested on 2 of 11 models.
  4. Agent tools (CoT variants, retrieval, a persistent notebook) help or hurt depending on the model — Llama-3-70B gains 92% relative accuracy from the Notebook tool while GPT-3.5 loses accuracy on every tool tried — so "add scaffolding" is not a universal prescription for medical agents.
